h1: Hefeweizen or witbier for a brewpub's first wheat beer
title: Hefeweizen or Witbier for a Brewpub | Craft Beer School
desc: A head brewer's comparison of hefeweizen and witbier for a brewpub: grist, yeast, process risk, tank time and which suits Indian drinkers and food.
teaser: Both are cloudy, both sell in the heat. One rides on yeast, the other on spice. Pick the one your brewhouse can repeat.
standfirst: Every Indian brewpub needs a wheat beer. The question is which one. Hefeweizen and witbier fill the same slot on the menu but demand different things from your grist, your yeast handling and your cellar. That should drive the choice.
sections:
Both beers are pale, hazy, lightly bitter and around 4.5 to 5.5% ABV. Both sell well in hot weather and both suit food. That is where the likeness stops.

A Bavarian hefeweizen gets nearly all of its character from yeast: banana from isoamyl acetate, clove from 4-vinyl guaiacol. There is no spice in the kettle. A Belgian witbier gets its signature from coriander seed and dried orange peel, with a softer, spicier yeast underneath and unmalted wheat for its pale, silky body. One is a fermentation beer. The other is a recipe beer. Our hefeweizen guide and witbier guide cover each in depth.

Hefeweizen. At least half the grist is malted wheat, often 50 to 70%, with Pilsner malt for the rest. German brewers have long used a ferulic acid rest around 43 to 45 °C to push clove character, then a step or single infusion for conversion. Wheat has no husk, so expect a slower lauter. Rice hulls at 2 to 5% of the grist are cheap insurance against a stuck mash.

Witbier. Typically around 40 to 50% unmalted wheat with Pilsner malt, sometimes a little oats. Raw wheat brings beta-glucans and more gumminess than malted wheat, so the lauter is the main risk. A protein or beta-glucan rest helps. Rice hulls again earn their place. The spice goes in late in the boil or whirlpool: coriander freshly cracked, not powdered. Use bitter orange peel rather than sweet.

This is where hefeweizen asks more of the brewer. The banana to clove balance moves with pitch rate, temperature and wort composition. Ferment warm and underpitch and you get banana bubblegum. Ferment cool around 17 to 18 °C and the clove comes forward. In a brewpub without tight glycol control, a hefeweizen can drift from batch to batch in a way regulars will notice.

Witbier yeast is more forgiving. Fermented around 18 to 22 °C it gives a gentle spicy, peppery character that blends with the coriander. If one batch runs a degree warm, the spice addition masks most of the difference. For a young team still building fermentation discipline, that tolerance matters.

Both are fast beers. Grain to glass in roughly two to three weeks is normal, with no long lagering. Neither should be filtered bright; the haze is part of the style. That means both beers are kind to a small cellar and turn tanks quickly, which is why they earn their place on an opening menu alongside the slower lager.

Ingredient cost differs a little. Witbier needs coriander and orange peel, which are easy to source in India and cheap at brewpub volumes. Hefeweizen needs a specific yeast strain that you will want to repitch carefully, since its character changes over generations. A sound yeast management programme is close to essential.
Which suits Indian drinkers and food

Hefeweizen has a head start in India. Many drinkers met wheat beer through Bavarian-style examples. The banana-clove profile is familiar on brewpub menus across Bengaluru, Pune and Gurugram. It works well with tandoori platters and fried snacks, where the carbonation and soft body cut through fat.

Witbier is the better match for lighter, citrus-led food: coastal fish, salads, chaat with lime and coriander. It also tends to appeal to drinkers who find hefeweizen's banana too sweet. Some brewpubs use witbier as their summer seasonal and keep hefeweizen year round.

If your fermentation control is solid and you can hold a tank within a degree, brew hefeweizen first. It sells on familiarity and rewards a skilled brewer with a beer drinkers return for. If the cellar is new, the team is still learning or the glycol system is shared with five other tanks, start with witbier. Its spice gives you room to learn without the beer changing under your feet.

Either way, write the recipe and the fermentation schedule down, taste every batch against the last and change one thing at a time. A house wheat beer that tastes the same in March and in October is worth more than a brilliant one that wanders.
faqs: Can I use the same yeast for hefeweizen and witbier?
You can, but neither beer will taste right. Hefeweizen needs a Bavarian weizen strain for banana and clove. Witbier needs a Belgian wit strain with its softer spice character.
Do I need unmalted wheat for witbier?
Traditional witbier uses unmalted wheat for its pale colour and silky body. Malted wheat works but gives a slightly different, breadier result. Plan your lauter around raw wheat if you use it.
Should a brewpub filter its wheat beer?
No. Both styles are served hazy, with yeast and wheat protein in suspension. Filtering strips flavour and mouthfeel along with the cloudiness.
